# Introduction
This analysis explores the **growth of Ethiopia’s ICT infrastructure from 2010 to 2024** using key World Bank indicators. By benchmarking Ethiopia against the Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) average, we examine **growth in internet penetration and mobile connectivity as well as their correlation with economic growth (GDP per capita).** This report specifically monitors progress toward *SDG 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure*

# Data Cleaning & Loading
All cleaning logic lives in a dedicated, fully commented script so that decisions (especially handling of missing values) are transparent and reproducible.
```
```{r data-loading}
# Run the cleaning pipeline (creates the tidy CSVs)
source("data_cleaning_script.R")

# Explicitly load the cleaned data into the analysis environment
df_long <- read_csv("digital_inclusion_clean_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
df_wide <- read_csv("digital_inclusion_clean_wide.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

message("Cleaned data loaded successfully.")
#message("df_long rows: ", nrow(df_long))
```
```{r data-cleaning2}
# Document missing values
missing_summary <- df_long %>%
  group_by(Indicator, Country) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Observations = n(),
    Missing_Values = sum(is.na(Value)),
    .groups = 'drop'
  ) %>%
  filter(Missing_Values > 0) %>%
  select(Indicator, Country, Missing_Values, Total_Observations)

# Print Missing Values Summary in a table
missing_summary %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Summary of Missing Data Points (2010-2024)")
```


# Visualizations

```{r plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=6.5, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
# Plot 1: Internet Penetration
p1 <- ggplot(df_long %>% filter(Indicator == "Individuals using the Internet (% of population)"),
       aes(x = Year, y = Value, color = Country, group = Country)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.3) + 
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2010, 2024, by = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Internet Penetration: Ethiopia vs Sub-Saharan Africa (2010–2024)",
       subtitle = "Individuals using the Internet (% of population)",
       y = "% of Population",
       x = "Year",
       caption = "Source: World Bank Development Indicators") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Ethiopia" = "#1f77b4", "Sub-Saharan Africa" = "#ff7f0e")) +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.15, 0.85), 
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "lightgrey"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 10, face = "italic")
  )
print(p1)
ggsave("plots/internet_penetration.png", plot = p1, width = 11, height = 6.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

# Plot 2: Mobile Subscriptions
p2 <- ggplot(df_long %>% filter(Indicator == "Mobile cellular subscriptions (per 100 people)", !is.na(Value)),
       aes(x = Year, y = Value, color = Country, group = Country)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.3) + 
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2010, 2024, by = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Mobile Cellular Subscriptions: Ethiopia vs Sub-Saharan Africa (2010–2024)",
       subtitle = "per 100 people",
       y = "Subscriptions per 100 people",
       x = "Year",
       caption = "Source: World Bank Development Indicators") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Ethiopia" = "#1f77b4", "Sub-Saharan Africa" = "#ff7f0e")) +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.85, 0.2), 
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "lightgrey"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 10, face = "italic")
  )
print(p2)
ggsave("plots/mobile_subscriptions.png", plot = p2, width = 11, height = 6.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

# Statistical Analysis - Linear Regression
We performed linear regression to measure the relationship between digital indicators and GDP per capita in both regions.

```{r regression}
ethiopia_wide <- df_long %>%
  filter(Country == "Ethiopia") %>%
  select(-Indicator_short) %>%          # ← this is the only change needed
  pivot_wider(names_from = Indicator, values_from = Value)

ssa_wide <- df_long %>%
  filter(Country == "Sub-Saharan Africa") %>%
  select(-Indicator_short) %>%          # ← this is the only change needed
  pivot_wider(names_from = Indicator, values_from = Value)
# Regression 1: Internet Penetration → GDP per capita - ETH
model1 <- lm(`GDP per capita (current US$)` ~ `Individuals using the Internet (% of population)`, data = ethiopia_wide)
# Regression 2: Mobile Subscriptions → GDP per capita - ETH
model2 <- lm(`GDP per capita (current US$)` ~ `Mobile cellular subscriptions (per 100 people)`, data = ethiopia_wide)
# Regression 3: Internet Penetration → GDP per capita - SSA
model3 <- lm(`GDP per capita (current US$)` ~ `Individuals using the Internet (% of population)`,data = ssa_wide)
# Regression 4: Mobile Subscriptions → GDP per capita - SSA
model4 <- lm(`GDP per capita (current US$)` ~ `Mobile cellular subscriptions (per 100 people)`,data = ssa_wide)

#Building tables using both 'tidy' and 'glance' data

# Helper function to combine Tidy and Glance stats
get_stats <- function(model, region_name) {
  t_stats <- tidy(model) %>% filter(term != "(Intercept)")
  g_stats <- glance(model)
  
  data.frame(
    Region = region_name,
    Estimate = t_stats$estimate,
    `P-Value` = t_stats$p.value,
    `R-Squared` = g_stats$r.squared
  )
}

# --- TABLE 1: Internet Penetration Comparison ---
internet_comparison <- bind_rows(
  get_stats(model1, "Ethiopia"),
  get_stats(model3, "Sub-Saharan Africa")
)

knitr::kable(internet_comparison, digits = 3, 
             caption = "Table 1: Comparison of Internet Penetration Impact on GDP")

# --- TABLE 2: Mobile Subscription Comparison ---
mobile_comparison <- bind_rows(
  get_stats(model2, "Ethiopia"),
  get_stats(model4, "Sub-Saharan Africa")
)

knitr::kable(mobile_comparison, digits = 3, 
             caption = "Table 2: Comparison of Mobile Subscription Impact on GDP")
```
## Statistical Interpretation - Understanding the Tables:

The regression analysis reveals **a strong and statistically significant positive relationship between digital access and GDP per capita in Ethiopia:**

**Internet Penetration:** A 1% increase is associated with a $32.95 increase in GDP per capita (R² = 0.876, p < 0.001).

**Mobile Subscriptions:** A 1% increase is associated with a $14.07 increase in GDP per capita (R² = 0.876, p < 0.001).

**Understanding the Metrics**

**R-squared (0.876):** 87.6% of the variation in Ethiopia’s GDP per capita can be explained by digital access indicators.

**P-value (< 0.001):** The results are highly statistically significant, meaning the observed relationships are very unlikely to be due to random chance.

In contrast, the same models for the Sub-Saharan Africa average show weak and statistically insignificant relationships.

**Methodological Note: Correlation vs. Causation**

While the models show a strong statistical fit, it is important to note that correlation does not imply causation. GDP per capita is influenced by many factors, including agriculture, foreign investment, trade, and political stability.

This analysi *does not claim that ICT is the sole driver of Ethiopia’s economic growth.* Rather, it demonstrates that digital access is a high-precision predictor and a powerful economic enabler. The data shows that digital transformation moves in near-perfect lockstep with national prosperity, even as other macroeconomic factors play their part.

**Limitations:** This analysis is based on aggregate national level data and does not account for urban-rural disparities or other macroeconomic variables. Regression results show association, not definitive causation.

# Key Insights

- **The Mobile-First Leap**
Ethiopia has experienced an aggressive upward trajectory in mobile connectivity, reaching over 65 subscriptions per 100 people by 2024.
  - *Analysis:* This steep growth curve suggests that the mobile phone has become the primary vehicle for digital and financial inclusion in the country. Unlike internet penetration, which requires more expensive devices and data plans, mobile subscriptions benefited from relatively lower barriers to entry. The data indicates that mobile infrastructure is currently delivering faster and broader reach than internet penetration, making it a foundational layer for Ethiopia’s digital economy.
- **The Lagged Dividend and the FinTech Catalyst (2021–2024)** 
The data shows that the initial 2018 telecommunication liberalization policy did not yield an immediate spike, but rather a gestation period followed by a vertical acceleration post 2020. 
  - *Analysis:* This reflects an Infrastructure Lag Effect, where the time required for capital expenditure and network densification delayed the visible impact of the 2018 reforms. However, the eventual surge was uniquely amplified by a second, independent data point: the launch of Telebirr in May 2021. By introducing mobile financial services at the same time as the improved infrastructure effect was exhibited, Ethiopia experienced a "perfect storm" of connectivity and utility. This suggests that liberalization provided the pipes, but FinTech provided the water that finally drove mass adoption and economic synchronization. 
- **Ethiopia as a Digital Growth Outlier**
A stark contrast exists between the domestic and regional models. While the Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) aggregate data is statistically "noisy" *(P > 0.40)* and shows almost no correlation with GDP *(R^2 < 0.06),* Ethiopia’s model is exceptionally precise *(P < 0.001, R^2 = 0.876).*
  - *Analysis:* The "noise" in the SSA average reflects the structural heterogeneity of the region—where diverse political shocks and commodity dependencies cancel each other out. In contrast, Ethiopia’s tight correlation proves its digital sector is a highly reliable and disciplined engine for economic expansion.
- **The "Multiplier Gap": Depth vs. Breadth**
While both Mobile and Internet growth explain 87.6% of Ethiopia’s GDP variance, the Economic Impact Estimate for Internet usage (32.95) is more than double that of Mobile subscriptions (14.06).
  - *Analysis:* This highlights the difference between Access (Mobile) and Utilization (Internet). While mobile phones provide the breadth of connectivity, internet penetration drives the depth of economic value. For every 1% growth, internet usage provides a 2.3x higher return on GDP per capita than basic mobile connectivity alone.
- **The Persistent Digital Divide**
Despite Ethiopia’s growth being more "efficient" and reliable than the regional average, an absolute gap remains. Ethiopia’s internet penetration (21.9%) still sits roughly 12 percentage points below the SSA average (33.6%).
  - *Analysis:* This "Catch-up Gap" represents an untapped economic frontier. Given the high multiplier effect of internet usage found in the regression models, closing this 12% gap could result in a significant, non-linear boost to Ethiopia's GDP per capita.
  
# Policy Recommendations
To accelerate digital transformation and close the remaining internet penetration gap, Ethiopia should prioritize affordable data tariffs, expanded rural broadband infrastructure, and targeted digital literacy programs. Shifting focus from basic mobile connectivity to meaningful internet usage will be essential to fully realize the strong economic returns associated with digital adoption.

Sustained telecom liberalization, combined with stronger integration of digital indicators into national planning, will enable more effective monitoring of SDG 9 progress and help translate connectivity gains into broader, inclusive economic growth.
